Volume 10 · Chapter 09

Greeks, volatility and hedging

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c08

By the endAnalyze hedge sensitivities and the implications of changing volatility assumptions.

Measure the exposure and finance the adjustment

Capability. Derive and interpret option Greeks, distinguish a partial sensitivity from a calibrated-price response, invert a vanilla price only within its valid volatility domain, and reconcile a discrete hedge with dividends, cash interest and trading fees. The prerequisite is Black–Scholes and risk-neutral valuation, including its funded dividend-adjusted PDE and vanilla formula. We use only the continuous-coefficient, localized Itô formula proved in Chapter 7; no general stochastic-volatility pricing theorem is assumed.

Oriole Risk sells calls and reports zero delta after buying shares. Its next-day loss is nevertheless large. A volatility quote changed, the stock moved enough for curvature to matter, and the share adjustment used cash. None contradicts a correctly calculated delta. A derivative describes one specified perturbation at one point. A hedge adds a trading rule, a funding rule and a model of what can change.

All prices, quotes and paths in this chapter are authored synthetic examples in currency units (CU). Time is in years. A vanilla contract covers one share until a stated multiplier is applied. Stock is ex-dividend; its continuous proportional payout rate is q, and its common borrowing/lending rate is r. These remain fixed in a quoted Greek unless explicitly changed. Actual contract rights, fees and funding access would have to be established separately before implementing the examples.

1. Derivatives with declared coordinates and units

Write τ = T − t and C(t,S;σ) for the Chapter 8 call with fixed strike K and maturity T. In the interior S,K,τ,σ > 0, let A = Se−qτ, H = Ke−rτ, a = σ√τ, d1 = [log(A/H) + a²/2]/a and d2 = d1 − a. Then C = AΦ(d1) − HΦ(d2). Here Φ and φ are the standard normal CDF and density. The identity Aφ(d1) = Hφ(d2) follows by subtracting their squared normal arguments, as proved in Chapter 8.

Fixed-parameter sensitivities of a single-share option
GreekDefinitionUse and scale
Delta Δ∂C/∂SShares of local stock exposure; Δ·dS has CU units
Gamma Γ∂²C/∂S²Change of delta per CU/share; ½Γ(dS)² is CU
Vega ν∂C/∂σCU per unit volatility parameter; a one-percentage-point change is dσ = 0.01
Calendar theta Θ∂C/∂t = −∂C/∂τCU/year for elapsed calendar time, with S and other parameters held fixed

The word “vega” is a market label, not a Greek-letter derivative convention that fixes its display units. This chapter reports ν per change of 1.00 in σ and also 0.01ν per volatility percentage point. Likewise, dividing annual theta by 252 or 365 is a chosen small-time reporting convention, not a new derivative and not necessarily a contract's day-count rule. A volatility change from 24% to 25% is one percentage point and a relative increase of about 4.17%; those are different perturbations.

Derive the formulas. Since ∂d1/∂S = ∂d2/∂S = 1/(Sa), the density terms cancel when differentiating C in S. Differentiating once more gives gamma. When differentiating in σ, A and H are constant and ∂d1/∂σ − ∂d2/∂σ = √τ; the same density identity leaves only that difference. Finally Aτ = −qA, Hτ = −rH and ∂τ(d1 − d2) = σ/(2√τ). Thus

ΔC = e−qτΦ(d1),   Γ = e−qτφ(d1)/(Sσ√τ),
ν = Se−qτφ(d1)√τ = S²στΓ,
ΘC = −Aφ(d1)σ/(2√τ) + qAΦ(d1) − rHΦ(d2).

Put–call parity C − P = A − H then gives ΔP = ΔC − e−qτ, ΓP = ΓC, νP = νC and ΘP = ΘC − qA + rH. Both vanilla gammas and vegas are strictly positive in the stated interior. A short position reverses their signs. Theta has no universal negative sign: the payout and funding terms can outweigh its negative diffusion term. The call delta remains distinct from the pricing exercise probability Φ(d2).

The identity ν = S²στΓ is useful for checking units and code, but does not make all portfolio risks interchangeable. It holds separately for a vanilla contract at its own σ and τ. Different maturities or fitted volatilities give different conversion factors. At the terminal payoff kink, interior derivatives do not apply. For S = K, r = q = 0 and fixed σ, as τ ↓ 0, gamma grows like 1/(Sσ√(2πτ)), vega shrinks like S√τ/√(2π), and theta's magnitude grows like Sσ/(2√(2πτ)). Away from the strike, the normal density can instead suppress these sensitivities. There is no uniform near-expiry Greek bound across all spots.

2. Position signs, hedge instruments and what zero delta means

For signed option quantities nj already including contract multipliers and h shares, marked portfolio delta is h + ΣnjΔj; gamma and vega are ΣnjΓj and Σnjνj. Set total stock holdings to −ΣnjΔj, trading −h − ΣnjΔj additional shares, to offset instantaneous stock sensitivity. Stock itself supplies no gamma or vega in this fixed-input mark calculation. Funding interest and dividend receipts still belong in the later cash ledger.

To offset both a portfolio gamma G and vega V with two options, solve Γ1x + Γ2y = −G and ν1x + ν2y = −V, then offset the resulting delta with shares. A unique solution requires Γ1ν2 − Γ2ν1 ≠ 0. If the two hedges share S, σ and τ, the preceding identity makes their gamma/vega columns proportional even when their strikes differ. They cannot span two arbitrary target exposures. A small determinant can require large offsetting positions; transaction costs, other Greeks, quote changes and position constraints remain after solving the linear equations.

Worked example 1 — A short call's positive theta is not a promised return

Oriole's single-share call has S = 120, K = 125, τ = 0.75, r = 0.03, q = 0.015 and σ = 0.24. The prepaid stock and discounted strike are 118.657565353 and 122.218904649; d1 = −0.038355277 and d2 = −0.246201373. Its price is 8.288309864 CU, with Δ = 0.479279867, Γ = 0.015804534, ν = 40.965350913 and calendar Θ = −7.168510612 CU/year. The put price is 11.849649160, with delta −0.509533177 and theta −5.281806952. Gamma and vega agree across the pair.

Sell 15 calls, each covering 100 shares: the option quantity is −1,500. The option position has delta −718.919801176 shares, gamma −23.706800297, vega −61,448.026370099 CU per unit σ, or −614.480263701 CU per volatility point. Buying 718.919801176 shares sets its initial delta to zero. Gamma and vega remain negative. Calendar theta is +10,752.765917465 CU/year, or a first-order +42.669706022 for 1/252 year with spot and σ frozen.

That last number is a conditional price change, not expected funded trading profit. The shares cost cash, their number will change, volatility may move, and curvature reacts to the stock's movement. Financing and dividend carry must be counted. A report that multiplies vega by “1” for a one-percentage-point volatility rise overstates this exposure by a factor of 100.

3. A local approximation needs a local error statement

At fixed r, q, K and T, a commonly used mark-change approximation is Δ·δS + ½Γ(δS)² + ν·δσ + Θ·δt. It is not the full second-order Taylor expansion in all three coordinates. It omits mixed derivatives such as CSσδSδσ, volatility curvature ½Cσσ(δσ)², and time cross terms. Those omissions can be second order, not third order.

For a precise statement take coordinates x = (t,S,σ), displacement h, and a line segment that remains in a compact interior region with positive remaining time, spot and volatility. Apply ordinary Taylor's theorem to g(u) = C(x + uh). If third partial derivatives are continuous there,

C(x+h) − C(x) = ∇C(x)·h + ½h′D²C(x)h + R,
|R| ≤ (1/6)Σa,b,cMabc|hahbhc|,

where Mabc bounds the absolute corresponding third derivative along the segment. This follows because g‴ is the sum of those derivative–displacement products. The units of each term agree. To bound the abbreviated Greek approximation, also bound the omitted Hessian terms by ½Σ(a,b)≠(S,S)Mab|hahb|. Merely sampling derivatives at a few points does not establish a supremum bound.

For a spot-only move h, we can supply an explicit conservative bound. Differentiating gamma gives CSSS = −(Γ/S)(1 + d1/a). On an interval [Smin,Smax] with other inputs fixed, d1 increases with S. Let D be the larger endpoint value of |d1|. Since φ ≤ 1/√(2π),

|CSSS| ≤ M3 := e−qτ[1+D/a]/[√(2π)Smin²a],
|C(S+h) − C(S) − Δh − ½Γh²| ≤ M3|h|³/6.

The bound is valid for puts too because their difference from the call is affine in S. It becomes weak near small τ or σ, exactly where a single local expansion can mislead. Crossing expiry or a payoff kink invalidates this smooth-region argument; repricing with the correct boundary contract is then essential.

Worked example 2 — A certified spot bound does not cover a mixed shock

Move the Worked example 1 spot from 120 to 123 with everything else fixed. Delta contributes 1.437839602 and gamma contributes 0.071120401, predicting 1.508960003 CU. Full formula repricing gives 1.508398767. The residual is about −0.000561237. The analytic interval bound above gives 0.000822669, so it covers the observed absolute residual without inferring a bound from that residual.

Now simultaneously increase σ by 0.015 and advance calendar time by 1/252 year. The vega and theta terms add 0.614480264 and −0.028446471. The abbreviated prediction is 2.094993796, whereas exact repricing gives 2.105551642, a residual 0.010557846. The spot-only bound does not cover this different perturbation. A proper bound needs the mixed/time/volatility derivative terms, or the changed contract must simply be repriced. More displayed decimal places do not recover omitted exposures.

4. A recalibrated surface changes the derivative being measured

Suppose a desk's declared scenario rule replaces fixed σ by a differentiable σ̂(S) for the same contract. Its reported mark is V(S) = C(S;σ̂(S)), so the ordinary chain rule gives

dV/dS = Δ + νσ̂S,
d²V/dS² = Γ + 2CSσσ̂S + Cσσ(σ̂S)² + νσ̂SS.

This is a total derivative along a specified repricing rule. The partial Black–Scholes delta still holds σ fixed. A cross-sectional skew σ̂(K) observed across strikes does not itself specify σ̂S as spot moves. Both dimensions and the rule connecting them matter. Different conventions about which quotes remain fixed under a shock can give different exposures; no convention is silently adopted here.

For the Oriole call, a stipulated local slope σ̂S = −0.0015 per CU changes total delta from 0.479279867 to 0.417831841. This does not prove that the slope will be realized or that the total derivative is a dynamic replication hedge. If fitted volatility evolves randomly, its own gains and cross-variation can matter. Deriving those terms requires an enlarged state model, not just substituting a different number in the fixed-σ hedge formula. Haugh's Greeks and volatility-surface notes offer further study; we use an explicit response rule instead of importing an unverified market convention.

5. Implied volatility is an inverse with a restricted domain

Fix S,K,τ > 0 and finite r,q, and view the vanilla call price as C(σ) for σ > 0. Its vega is strictly positive, so C is strictly increasing. As σ ↓ 0, d1 and d2 tend together to the sign of log(A/H) times infinity when A ≠ H; at A = H they tend to zero. The resulting lower limit is L = max(A − H,0). As σ → ∞, d1 → ∞ and d2 → −∞, so C → A. Consequently continuity and the intermediate-value theorem give:

A unique finite positive implied volatility exists exactly when L < Cquote < A.

At the lower bound the nonnegative-volatility extension has σ = 0, not a positive solution. At the upper bound no finite σ exists. Outside [L,A] the quote is inconsistent with this vanilla inversion and the stated inputs. For a put the corresponding interval is (max(H − A,0),H), with the same implied σ as a parity-matched call. At τ = 0, S = 0, or K = 0 where the payoff price loses its σ dependence, this strict theorem is unavailable: a matching price need not identify volatility at all. An American quote or a fixed-cash-dividend contract is not converted into this European proportional-yield contract by running a root solver.

Existence is not numerical precision. At a positive interior solution, differentiating C(σ) = c gives dσ/dc = 1/ν. More strongly, if ν(σ) ≥ m > 0 throughout an interval containing two solutions, the mean-value theorem proves |σ2 − σ1| ≤ |c2 − c1|/m. Vega at one endpoint is not automatically a valid lower bound. Short maturities and extreme moneyness can make price changes tiny relative to volatility changes; near the upper limit vega also vanishes. Exact uniqueness can coexist with a practically uninformative quote interval.

A robust finite routine first checks the contract and price bounds, then obtains σlo,σhi with C(σlo) ≤ c ≤ C(σhi). Monotonicity preserves that bracket under bisection: replace the lower endpoint when the midpoint price is below c and the upper endpoint otherwise. After n updates the width is the initial width divided by 2n, using exact comparisons. With finite-precision prices, comparisons and residuals have a numerical resolution too. A small price residual alone is insufficient when vega is tiny. Report the bracket width, residual, units, cap and conditioning; use a bounded iteration count and do not claim a root outside the searched interval.

Worked example 3 — Quote precision and inverse precision are different

For Oriole's S = 120, K = 125 and remaining contract terms, an invented call quote of 11.05 lies strictly between 0 and 118.657565353. Searching σ ∈ [0,2] takes 35 bisections to reduce the width below 10−10. The lab returns σ ≈ 0.307377471676, computed bracket [0.307377471647, 0.307377471705], and price residual about −8.0×10−10 CU. This is approximately 30.737747%, not 0.307377%.

Vega at that solution is approximately 40.985568069. Locally, a one-cent quote change moves σ by about 0.01/40.985568069 = 0.000243988, or 0.0243988 volatility percentage points. That quote uncertainty is millions of times larger than the solver's stopping width. A numerical bracket is not a confidence interval and does not remove bid/ask, dividend or funding uncertainty.

The lab uses a declared price-resolution band of 10−11max(1,A,H). An interior quote within that band of a price boundary returns an unresolved_near_price_boundary status. An exact lower-bound quote returns the zero-volatility limit; an exact upper bound has no finite solution. A quote above the price attainable at the configured σ cap returns root_above_declared_sigma_cap. None is converted to a fabricated calibrated volatility. The computed bracket is a floating-point numerical result, not an interval-arithmetic proof.

6. Test prices before interpreting a smile

A smile is a cross-section of fitted σ values that varies with strike; a skew emphasizes an asymmetric slope. A maturity dimension makes a surface. These describe how quotes are represented through a chosen formula. They do not by themselves estimate physical volatility, identify a unique stochastic mechanism or establish an arbitrage-free dynamic process. Even a unique implied volatility for each individual quote does not make the collection jointly coherent.

For matched European calls at one maturity and discount D = e−rτ, payoff inequalities from Chapter 6 imply, for K1 < K2, −D ≤ [C(K2) − C(K1)]/(K2 − K1) ≤ 0. For K1 < K2 < K3, let λ = (K3 − K2)/(K3 − K1). Statewise convexity in strike gives

λC(K1) + (1 − λ)C(K3) − C(K2) ≥ 0.

Long the two endpoint calls in these weights and short the middle call. Their terminal weighted butterfly is nonnegative; a negative purchase cost gives an initial receipt with no later negative payoff under matched executable rights. The proof is a cash-payoff comparison, not a claim that every violation of a mid-quote screen can be traded after spreads, fees and size limits. Passing these finite-strike tests is necessary, not sufficient for every missing strike, maturity and dynamic consistency condition. We do not extrapolate a full stochastic process from three passing prices.

Worked example 4 — All three inversions succeed and the quote set still fails

In a separate zero-rate, zero-yield, one-year market with S = 100, invented calls at strikes 90, 100 and 110 cost 14, 11 and 5. Each satisfies its strict individual bounds and has a positive implied volatility, approximately 21.243759%, 27.660842% and 21.887379%. Prices decrease with strike, and adjacent slopes −0.3 and −0.6 lie between −1 and 0.

The slopes nevertheless decrease rather than increase, violating convexity. One call at 90, minus two calls at 100, plus one at 110 costs 14 − 22 + 5 = −3 CU. Its payoff is zero outside [90,110] and a nonnegative triangle inside, peaking at 10. The normalized half-sized version used by the lab costs −1.5. Thus a successful root solve at every strike does not validate the smile. Lowering only the middle price to 9 makes the same finite convexity test pass, but still does not identify dynamics or prices for unobserved contracts.

7. A discrete delta hedge is a cash-account recursion

Consider a portfolio H intended to cover one written call, initially funded by the model premium C0. At reset date ti, hold ni = Δ(ti,Si;σ̄) shares and bank value bi = Hi − niSi. Keep σ̄ fixed. Between reset dates, specify that all proportional dividends are reinvested continuously in stock without friction. This mechanical rule grows the share count to nieq hi; signed short shares require the corresponding dividend compensation. Bank value becomes bier hi, where hi = ti+1 − ti. No endpoint approximation to dividend cash is needed.

Hi+1− = nieqhᵢSi+1 + bierhᵢ,
tradei+1 = [ni+1 − nieqhᵢ]Si+1,
bi+1 = bierhᵢ − tradei+1 − feei+1.

Consequently H after a costless reset equals H before it. With a fee it falls by that fee, financed through cash rather than an unexplained external contribution. Crucially, do not replace H by the newly calculated option mark. Setting b = Cnew − ΔnewS would inject or withdraw Cnew − H and erase the hedge error being measured. At maturity liquidate stock and bank, subtract the call payoff, and record HT − (ST − K)+. A negative result is a remaining obligation, even if all preceding rebalances were self-financing.

Worked example 5 — Gains on one path do not certify the hedge

Use the Oriole call, with prices 120, 126, 113 and 130 at dates 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. Initially hold 0.479279867 shares and borrow 49.225274230 CU; the net portfolio costs 8.288309864. At the first reset, dividend reinvestment leaves 0.481080541 shares and debt has grown to 49.595851716. Wealth is 11.020296464, while the option mark is only 9.386277452.

The new delta is 0.565595070. Buying the difference costs 10.648830694, so ideal debt becomes 60.244682410. At date 0.5, incoming shares are 0.567720034 and bank is −60.698216154. Selling down to delta 0.225839301 receives 38.632522755, leaving bank −22.065693398. Neither reset forces wealth back to the call mark.

At maturity the shares have grown to 0.226687789 and bank is −22.231808251. Liquidation at 130 leaves 7.237604281; the call owes 5, leaving error +2.237604281. Add a 0.2% fee on the absolute stock-trade cash at each interior reset only. The two fees are 0.021297661 and 0.077265046; separately accumulated to maturity they total 0.099466246. The funded final error is therefore +2.138138035.

Change only the last price from 130 to 95. The call now expires worthless, but the portfolio liquidates to −0.696468323 before fees or −0.795934570 after them. The earlier holdings and debt do not change retroactively. These authored paths establish neither a return distribution nor an expected profit; they demonstrate that a discrete hedge can have either sign of error and that its debt must be honored.

8. Derive the continuous volatility-mismatch identity with its funding

There is a useful continuous benchmark, but its assumptions are different from a list of observed price changes. Suppose an actual positive continuous process on [0,T] satisfies dS = μtSdt + atSdW, with continuous adapted μ and a, and the same constant r and q as the pricing inputs. Existence of this process is assumed, not derived for arbitrary coefficient functions. Use the fixed positive pricing volatility σ̄ in the smooth vanilla mark C and continuously hold Δ = CS. Let H obey the funded gains equation dH = Δ(dS + qSdt) + r(H − ΔS)dt. Define the writer's hedging error E = H − C.

Apply the proved localized scalar Itô formula before T. Its diffusion term ΔatS cancels between H and C, as does μtSΔ. The PDE for C uses σ̄, whereas its actual Itô second-order term uses at. Subtracting and using the product rule with e−rt gives

dE = rE dt + ½ΓS²(σ̄² − at²)dt,
e−rtEt = E0 + ∫0t½e−ruΓ(u,Su;σ̄)Su²(σ̄² − au²)du.

This includes financing. Omitting the discount inside the integral and the terminal accumulation outside it is generally wrong when r ≠ 0. If H0 = C0, E0 = 0. The opposite, long-option-minus-replica position reverses the sign.

The identity extends pathwise to T in the stated continuous-coefficient setting. For the laboratory's nonnegative q, on each compact path S and a have finite maxima, while ΓS² ≤ S/[σ̄√(2π(T−t))]. Multiplying by bounded pathwise coefficients and integrating 1/√(T−t) gives a finite absolute integral. Also 0 ≤ Δ ≤ 1, so localizing the bounded-on-path coefficients S, μ and a makes both the drift integral and the squared stochastic integrand integrable through T. The funded gains therefore have a continuous terminal extension even if delta has no terminal limit at the strike. The vanilla mark tends to its continuous payoff, completing the pathwise identity. For a finite negative q the same argument uses the extra uniform factor e|q|T. To average the identity over paths one needs additional integrability, for example a finite expectation of the displayed supremum bound.

For a short vanilla option hedged under these ideal rights, at² ≤ σ̄² at every time makes the error nonnegative because Γ is positive. An unweighted average variance comparison alone cannot determine the sign when the discrepancy changes sign: discounted cash gamma ½e−rtΓS² varies along the path. As a purely algebraic accounting example, two half-year slices with supplied discounted cash-gamma weights 50 and 200, σ̄ = 0.25, and actual variance levels 0.09 and 0.04 give 1.5625 CU discounted error. Reversing the two variance levels gives −2.1875, although both time-average variances are 0.065. These supplied weights illustrate the integral's weighting; they are not claimed to reconstruct two actual diffusion trajectories.

Discrete resetting introduces additional error. With no fee and a freshly matched H = C, a short-interval expansion gives approximately ½Γ[σ̄²S²h − (δS)²], plus higher-order spot/time terms and any other changed input. This follows by subtracting the Taylor mark change from the funded stock/cash increment and using the PDE for theta. Terms such as h·δS, h² and the spatial Taylor remainder have not vanished. The finite sum is not an exact realized-variance identity. Jumps, recalibrated σ, different financing or payout terms, and trading fees change the argument; their effects cannot be absorbed by asserting “realized volatility was lower.”

9. Differentiate carefully and validate the perturbation

A central price difference [C(S+h) − C(S−h)]/(2h) has delta error at most M3h²/6 when the third spatial derivative is bounded by M3 on that interval. Expand both sides through second order; the even terms cancel and the two third-order remainders give the bound. If each evaluated price has absolute error at most ε, an additional error at most ε/h follows by the triangle inequality. Smaller h reduces truncation while amplifying price error.

For gamma, [C(S+h) − 2C(S) + C(S−h)]/h² has error at most M4h²/12 + 4ε/h² under a fourth-derivative bound. This follows from Taylor expansion through third order and the coefficients 1,−2,1. Neither expression guarantees accuracy without its smoothness and price-error assumptions. Comparing several well-scaled h values, analytical identities, independent payoff integration and boundary cases is more informative than picking the smallest representable h. Haugh's sensitivity-estimation notes, Section 1, discuss finite-difference perturbations and additional sampling issues. The present lab is deterministic; Monte Carlo error belongs to the next chapter's analysis.

Reproducible sensitivities and cash laboratory

Download the original inputs, standard-library model, reference output, instructions and domain, and four-file integrity manifest. The seven reports cover base Greeks, signed exposures, shocks, implied-volatility inversion, a same-expiry quote screen, a dividend-reinvestment hedge and supplied-weight variance accounting. Strict bounds and finite iteration limits keep the task reproducible. Financial arithmetic uses double precision with explicit comparison tolerances; no claim of exact decimal prices is made.

Before running it, predict the effects of reversing the option position, setting fees to zero, changing only the final spot, lowering the middle smile quote, narrowing the volatility cap, and interchanging the two variance levels. Explain which neighboring reports should remain unchanged. The output is implementation evidence for a conditional model, not empirical validation or an instruction to trade.

Exercises

State units, held-fixed inputs, signs and funding dates. Proof requirements must be answered analytically; numbers alone do not establish them. Exercise 10 accepts different research designs when they meet its criteria.

  1. Derive and transfer the Greeks. Derive delta, gamma, vega and calendar theta from the vanilla formula using the density identity. Prove ν = S²στΓ and give the put adjustments from parity. Then evaluate the call and put and their Greeks at S = 85, K = 90, τ = 0.5, r = 0.01, q = 0.02, σ = 0.30. Report vega both per unit σ and per volatility percentage point.
  2. A hedge can span too few exposures. A portfolio risk report gives delta −100 shares, gamma −6 and vega −12,000 CU per unit σ. A single-share hedge option has delta 0.6, gamma 0.02 and vega 30 in the same units. Treat these supplied coefficients as exact for this linear worksheet. Choose its quantity and the stock trade to remove gamma and delta, then compute residual vega and first-order mark change for a 0.01 volatility increase. Prove why two same-σ, same-expiry vanilla hedge options cannot span arbitrary gamma and vega targets using their strikes alone.
  3. Bound the approximation you actually used. Derive CSSS = −(Γ/S)(1 + d1/a) and the stated interval bound. Recompute the Oriole spot-only 120→123 Taylor change and bound. Then explain why adding a volatility move and elapsed time invalidates applying that spot-only bound to the full residual; identify the missing second-order terms.
  4. Partial and total derivatives. At a contract, fixed-input delta is 0.5 and vega is 30. A stated calibration rule has σ̂S = −0.002 volatility units per CU. Find total delta and derive the total-gamma formula, naming every partial derivative held fixed. Does a downward cross-sectional skew in strike prove that this slope in spot is negative? Explain the identification problem.
  5. Invert on the correct domain. Prove the exact positive-implied-volatility range for S,K,τ > 0. In the zero-rate, zero-yield case S = K = 80 and τ = 0.25, a quote is 80[2Φ(0.1) − 1]. Find its implied σ without numerical root finding. Classify quotes 0, 80 and 81 and the same pricing task at expiry. If vega is known to be at least 2 throughout a solution interval and price uncertainty is at most 0.05, prove the corresponding volatility-distance bound and distinguish it from a one-point derivative estimate.
  6. Audit the actual bank account. Reconstruct the first Oriole hedge reset, including reinvested dividend shares, accumulated debt and stock trade. Explain the cash transfer required if someone instead resets bank to Cnew − ΔnewS. Change only the final spot to 95, keeping the previous two resets and fees. Compute terminal ideal and fee-funded errors, and independently reconcile the difference using separately compounded fee payments.
  7. Variance mismatch with a funded position. Under the continuous positive-diffusion assumptions in Section 8, derive the discounted error identity for H − C and justify its terminal pathwise limit. Compute the supplied-weight two-slice result for weights (50,200), durations (0.5,0.5), model σ = 0.25 and actual σ values (0.30,0.20), then reverse their order. Explain why equal unweighted average variance does not make the results equal and why neither calculation alone is an exact discrete hedge experiment.
  8. Unequally spaced strike audit. In a separate S = 100, r = q = 0, τ = 1 market, calls at strikes 90, 100 and 115 quote 17, 13 and 5. Verify their individual bounds and decreasing prices. Construct the normalized weighted butterfly for the uneven spacing, give its initial cost and its terminal payoff on the four strike intervals. Does fitting an individual implied volatility to each quote cure the violation?
  9. Choose a perturbation with an error budget. Prove the central-delta error bound M3h²/6 + ε/h and the central-gamma bound M4h²/12 + 4ε/h². For M3 = 0.003 CU−2 and absolute price error ε = 10−6 CU, minimize the delta bound over h > 0 and evaluate its minimum. State the additional requirement before using that h near an option boundary.
  10. Research and model critique. A desk memo says: “Zero delta removes risk. Positive short-option theta is expected daily profit. A fitted smile validates the volatility process. A tiny inversion residual identifies σ precisely. Realized variance below implied variance guarantees a profit for every discrete delta hedge, including fees.” Correct each claim. Design an out-of-sample hedge and quote-validation protocol with frozen trading and surface-response rules, concrete data requirements, at least two quantitative examples from this chapter, an independent numerical check, and explicit limits on what the evidence can establish.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Cancel density terms before differentiating again

    The S derivatives of d1,d2 coincide; Aφ(d1) = Hφ(d2) cancels their contributions to CS, leaving e−qτΦ(d1). Its S derivative is e−qτφ(d1)/(Sσ√τ). For σ, only the normal terms vary; their derivative difference is √τ, yielding ν = Aφ(d1)√τ = S²στΓ. For τ, differentiate A and H and use (d1 − d2)τ = σ/(2√τ), then negate to obtain calendar theta. Parity supplies put delta ΔC − e−qτ, equal gamma/vega and ΘP = ΘC − qA + rH.

    The transfer values are C = 4.949425248, P = 10.346312506, call/put deltas 0.421612037 and −0.568437797, gamma 0.021525460, vega 23.328217770 per unit σ or 0.233282178 per volatility point, and call/put calendar thetas −6.590600847 and −7.378174333 CU/year. Differentiating in remaining maturity instead would reverse the two theta signs.

  2. Count instruments and independent directions

    Gamma neutrality requires −6 + 0.02x = 0, so buy 300 hedge-option units. Their delta 180 changes total delta to +80, requiring 80 shares sold. Residual vega is −12,000 + 300(30) = −3,000 CU per unit σ, so a 0.01 volatility rise contributes approximately −30 CU, even at zero delta and gamma. These are local marked exposures and omit the financed cost of acquiring the positions.

    For same S, σ and τ, each vanilla hedge has νj = S²στΓj. Thus Γ1ν2 − Γ2ν1 = 0. The two equations are linearly dependent, so an arbitrary target pair may have no solution; a compatible target can have many. Stock adds delta but no independent gamma/vega direction. Changing strike alone does not remove this rank problem.

  3. The mixed shock has additional second-order terms

    Differentiate Γ = e−qτφ(d1)/(Sa), use φ′ = −d1φ and d1,S = 1/(Sa), and combine the density and 1/S derivatives to obtain −Γ(1 + d1/a)/S. Bounding φ by 1/√(2π), S below by Smin, and |d1| by its endpoint maximum gives the displayed M3. Taylor's one-variable remainder is then at most M3|h|³/6.

    For h = 3, Δh + ½Γh² = 1.508960003; exact change is 1.508398767, with error approximately −0.000561237 and analytic absolute bound 0.000822669. A mixed shock additionally includes CSσδSδσ, ½Cσσ(δσ)², CStδSδt, Cσtδσδt and ½Ctt(δt)², plus the full third-order remainder. The mixed Oriole residual 0.010557846 is not evidence against the valid spot-only bound; it belongs to a different expression.

  4. Name the path through parameter space

    Total delta is 0.5 + 30(−0.002) = 0.44. Differentiate CS + Cσσ̂S again along σ̂(S). The result is CSS + 2CSσσ̂S + Cσσ(σ̂S)² + Cσσ̂SS. Each C partial treats its other coordinates, strike, maturity, r and q as fixed. The two cross terms come from differentiating both CS and Cσ.

    A skew in strike measures ∂σ̂/∂K at the current snapshot, not its future response ∂σ̂/∂S for a fixed contract. Several dynamic response rules can match the same snapshot. Historical estimation or a declared scenario convention can supply a rule, but the cross-section alone does not identify it or establish replication under it.

  5. The inverse theorem has strict interior endpoints

    For σ > 0, ν = Aφ(d1)√τ > 0, so C is strictly increasing and continuous. Its zero-volatility and infinite-volatility limits are L and A, proved by the normal-argument limits. The intermediate-value theorem gives existence for every quote strictly between them; strict increase gives uniqueness, and the endpoint limits exclude any other finite positive solution.

    At S = K and zero carry, d1 = σ√τ/2 and d2 = −d1, so the specified quote 6.372453964 CU requires σ√0.25/2 = 0.1, hence σ = 0.40. Quote 0 is the zero-volatility limit; 80 is the unattained finite-volatility upper bound; 81 violates the individual bound. At expiry the call price is the payoff 0 for every σ, so a matching zero quote does not identify volatility. By the mean-value theorem, |δσ| ≤ 0.05/2 = 0.025, or 2.5 volatility percentage points, provided the positive lower-vega bound holds throughout the solution interval. Substituting only the initial vega into a differential gives a local approximation, not that finite bound.

  6. A forced mark reset is an external transfer

    After 0.25 years, incoming shares are 0.479279867451e0.015·0.25 = 0.481080541107 and bank is −49.225274230380e0.03·0.25 = −49.595851715597. Wealth at 126 is 11.020296463864. Buying to delta 0.565595070427 costs 10.648830694279, so the costless bank becomes −60.244682409876. Stock plus bank preserves wealth.

    Resetting instead to the option mark 9.386277452133 would withdraw 1.634019011730 CU from the hedge. That is an external distribution and must be recorded; silently doing it is not the specified retained-cash strategy. With the final price changed to 95, pre-liquidation shares remain 0.226687788708 and bank −22.231808250672. The payoff is zero, giving ideal error −0.696468323447. Fee cost at maturity is 0.021297661389e0.03·0.5 + 0.077265045511e0.03·0.25 = 0.099466246196. Subtracting gives −0.795934569643. Future price changes cannot finance past trades retroactively.

  7. Gamma weights the variance discrepancy

    Subtract actual-path Itô gains dC = [Ct + μSΔ + ½a²S²Γ]dt + ΔaS dW from dH = [μSΔ + qSΔ + r(H−SΔ)]dt + ΔaS dW. The diffusion and μ terms cancel. The model PDE replaces −Ct − (r−q)SΔ by ½σ̄²S²Γ − rC, leaving d(H−C) = r(H−C)dt + ½S²Γ(σ̄²−a²)dt. The bank discount product rule proves the integral formula.

    For the terminal limit, continuous actual S,a are bounded on each compact path. The vanilla bound ΓS² ≤ S/[σ̄√(2π(T−t))] gives an absolutely integrable pathwise majorant for the discrepancy; ∫0T(T−t)−1/2dt = 2√T. Continuity of the financed gains and terminal payoff completes the pathwise limit. An expectation statement needs its own integrable random domination.

    The first worksheet gives 0.5[50(0.0625−0.09) + 200(0.0625−0.04)] = 1.5625. Reversing variance levels gives 0.5[50(0.0625−0.04) + 200(0.0625−0.09)] = −2.1875. Both average variances equal 0.065, but the weighted averages differ. Supplied piecewise weights do not prove the existence of particular joint stock/volatility paths, and discrete resets, fees or jumps add effects outside the ideal continuous identity.

  8. Weights follow strike spacing

    The individual call intervals are (10,100), (0,100) and (0,100); all three quotes lie inside and decline with strike. The lower and upper endpoint weights are 15/25 = 0.6 and 10/25 = 0.4. Buy 0.6 calls at 90 and 0.4 at 115 and write one at 100. Cost is 0.6(17) + 0.4(5) − 13 = −0.8 CU.

    The payoff is zero at ST ≤ 90; 0.6(ST−90) on [90,100]; 0.4(115−ST) on [100,115]; and zero above 115. It is nonnegative and peaks at 6. This is an initial receipt with no negative terminal cash under matched executable rights. Individual implied-volatility fits reproduce these same offending prices, so they do not remove the joint violation. The adjacent slopes −0.4 and −8/15 also display decreasing rather than increasing slope.

  9. Balance truncation and evaluation error

    Expand C(S±h) through second order, bound each third-order remainder by M3h³/6 and divide their difference by 2h. The derivative error is at most M3h²/6. Two price errors each bounded by ε add at most 2ε/(2h) = ε/h. For gamma, expand through third order; odd terms cancel, two fourth-order remainders contribute M4h⁴/12, and evaluation errors have total coefficient magnitude 1+2+1 = 4. Division by h² yields the stated bound.

    Differentiating B(h) = M3h²/6 + ε/h gives B′ = M3h/3 − ε/h². Its sole positive zero is h = (3ε/M3)1/3; B″ > 0 proves the minimum. The supplied numbers give h = 0.1 CU and bound 0.000015 in delta units: 0.000005 truncation plus 0.000010 evaluation. The entire [S−h,S+h] interval must remain in the smooth domain where the derivative bound holds. The assumed ε must describe the actual pricing evaluation; it cannot be guessed from the number of displayed digits.

  10. Validate the perturbation, the cash and the empirical claim separately

    Zero delta removes only the specified first-order spot exposure; gamma, vega, funding, basis and execution risks can remain. Positive short-option theta is a held-fixed mark sensitivity, not a physical expected funded return. Individual smile inversions need joint price tests and still do not identify dynamics. A tiny residual can hide a large inverse-volatility uncertainty when vega is small; quote and input errors remain even after numerical convergence. The continuous variance identity has gamma weights and matching diffusion/funding assumptions, while a discrete hedge has reset errors and fees.

    Quantitative corrections include Oriole's −614.480263701 CU per volatility point despite initial delta neutrality; the −3 CU butterfly cost after three successful inversions; quote 11.05 moving σ by about 0.0243988 volatility percentage points per cent; discrete hedge errors +2.138138035 and −0.795934570 on the two fee-funded paths; or the equal-average-variance worksheet giving opposite signs. Explain at least two with units and the relevant contract assumptions.

    A feasible protocol freezes a versioned pricing implementation, contemporaneous bid/ask and size data, strike/expiry and payout rights, funding curve, dividend assumptions, volatility-response rule, reset calendar and executable fee schedule. Run independent payoff integration, finite-difference scale tests, parity, strike-spread/convexity checks and inverse-bracket checks before empirical evaluation. Select the out-of-sample dates and contracts in advance, then reconcile every dividend, stock trade, cash interest and option settlement; retain failed trades and missed calls rather than selecting successful paths. Compare hedge errors by maturity, moneyness, event exposure and trading cost, and distinguish parameter/input errors from residual model risk.

    Evaluation. Full credit requires correcting all five claims; two correct numerical examples; explicit coordinates, trading and calibration rules; independent numerical and joint-price checks; a reproducible out-of-sample cash evaluation; and limits on causal or dynamic inference. The scoped primary readings provide mathematical background, not evidence that these synthetic paths represent a market. Alternative study designs are acceptable if their target, selection rules and uncertainty are explicit. A passing benchmark does not guarantee future hedge performance.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a treasurer why “we are delta neutral and sold high implied volatility” is an incomplete risk report. Distinguish a derivative, a repricing convention, a trading strategy and a cash obligation.

Model answer. Delta refers to a specified held-fixed perturbation and does not remove curvature or volatility exposure. A recalibration rule may change the total spot response. Selling a high quoted σ does not identify future gamma-weighted variance or cover discrete reset errors. The hedge must specify when shares change, how dividends are used and how trades, interest and fees are paid. Its terminal error must be reconciled against the option obligation, including any remaining debt.

Delayed retention, after 7–14 days. (i) A position has vega −2,400 per unit σ: find the first-order effect of a two-volatility-point rise. (ii) At S = 100, σ = 0.20, τ = 0.5 and gamma 0.03, find vanilla vega. (iii) What happens to a zero-delta portfolio's gamma when stock alone is added? (iv) Classify a European call quote equal to its prepaid-stock upper bound at positive S,K,τ. (v) If a funded hedge has incoming wealth 7, the new model mark is 6 and a stock reset costs 2, how should the bank change without an external distribution?

Answers. (i) −2,400(0.02) = −48 CU. (ii) S²στΓ = 10000(0.20)(0.5)(0.03) = 30 per unit σ, or 0.30 per volatility point. (iii) Stock changes delta but not the option gamma in this mark calculation. (iv) No finite positive implied volatility achieves that upper limit. (v) Deduct 2 from the incoming bank; total wealth remains 7 before any fee. Forcing wealth to 6 would withdraw 1 and must be recorded. Advancement requires these answers, the inverse-domain proof and a fresh funded hedge ledger.

Sources and further development

Martin Haugh, The Black–Scholes Model (2016), Sections 2–4, is further reading on Greeks, implied-volatility representation and hedging. We derive our own inverse bounds, controlled approximation and explicitly discounted funding identity; no current convention or empirical generalization from those historical notes is assumed. Haugh, Estimating the Greeks (2017), Section 1, is a further route to sensitivity estimation. Its simulation estimators and examples are not reproduced here.

Numerical pricing and Monte Carlo develops approximation, sampling and stability questions. Incomplete markets and advanced derivatives then enlarges the set of risks and contracts. A fitted vanilla surface, a local Greek hedge and a validated implementation are useful pieces of evidence; each has a stated scope rather than supplying all of those later results.
